metadata.description: Free, tested Agent Skills and subagents for higher-ed faculty, administrators, and independent consultants.

plugins.name: educator-essentials-pack
plugins.description: The teaching wave in one install: the assessment suite, the feedback and letters pair, and the responsible-AI pair — eight coordinated skills that share vocabulary and update together.

plugins.name: second-brain-starter-pack
plugins.description: A working second brain in a box: a wrap-up skill that persists what each session learned, a librarian agent that answers from your notes, and a devil's-advocate agent that pressure-tests your decisions. Requires an agentic surface (Claude Code or Cowork).

plugins.name: ai-guidelines-workshop
plugins.description: A process companion for writing AI guidelines for a team, department, or program — not a document generator. Drafting the document is the easy part; the process is where efforts stall, across stakeholders, feedback rounds, and revisions over weeks. This keeps the working state of the effort — stakeholder map, decision log, open questions, draft-in-progress — so every session starts where the last one ended, and drafts with a three-camps diagnostic and an augmentation-spectrum backbone. Use when developing AI guidelines, an AI policy, or usage principles for an organization. Trigger phrases include "write AI guidelines for my department", "develop an AI policy", "AI usage principles", "our team needs AI guidelines", "resume the guidelines draft".

plugins.name: ai-use-disclosure
plugins.description: Drafts an honest, right-sized statement of how AI was actually used in a piece of work, matched to where it's going — a journal, a classroom, a workplace. It reconstructs how AI actually contributed during the session (ideation, drafting, editing, verification) and writes a disclosure sized to the venue's norms, from a one-line note to a formal statement. It's a finishing pass: spell-check at the end, not autocorrect while you type. Use when a piece is ready to ship and needs an AI-use statement, acknowledgment, or disclosure. Trigger phrases include "write an AI disclosure", "how do I disclose AI use", "AI use statement", "acknowledge AI in this", "disclosure for this paper".

plugins.name: assessment-ai-policy-writer
plugins.description: Sets clear AI expectations one assessment at a time. For each task it places the work on an augmentation spectrum (from no-AI to full collaboration), decides what's allowed, off-limits, and must be disclosed — each with the pedagogical reason — and writes student-facing policy language in plain English. When the term's assessments each have a policy, it rolls them up into a coherent syllabus section. Use when writing an AI policy for an assignment or course, deciding what AI use to allow, or drafting syllabus AI language. Trigger phrases include "AI policy for this assignment", "what AI use should I allow", "syllabus AI statement", "can students use AI on this", "write my AI policy".

plugins.name: assessment-redesigner
plugins.description: Redesigns an assignment for the age of AI. Hand it an assessment that AI can now produce convincing work for, and it maps which parts AI has made trivial, names what the task was really trying to measure, and rebuilds it so the student's thinking is visible again — working through a five-category redesign framework, fitted to your class size, modality, and grading capacity. Use when an assignment feels newly defeatable ("students can just use ChatGPT for this"), when rethinking a whole course's assessments, or when you want to move past detection and bans to redesign. Trigger phrases include "redesign this assignment", "make this AI-resistant", "AI-proof my assessment", "rethink my assessments", "students can just use AI for this", "assessment redesign".

plugins.name: confusion-forecaster
plugins.description: Reads instructional material the way the most literal capable student will, and hands back a ranked confusion forecast before you publish — so you fix the unclear instruction now instead of discovering it in a week of student emails. Feed it an assignment sheet, lesson plan, syllabus section, rubric, or module page; it does a cold first-read, flags every ambiguity, hidden prerequisite, ordering problem, and load spike, ranks them by how many emails each will actually generate, and proposes the smallest edit that removes each one without touching your voice. Use when drafting or revising anything students will read and follow on their own. Trigger phrases include "is this assignment clear", "will students understand this", "proofread my instructions", "check my assignment sheet", "did I explain this well", "before I post this to the LMS", "read this like a student", "why is everyone confused about".

plugins.name: feedback-first-pass
plugins.description: Drafts formative feedback on student work in your voice and against your rubric, so your time goes to judgment instead of typing. On first run it learns your voice from 2–3 real samples of feedback you've written; then it drafts per-student comments tied to your rubric criteria — for one submission or a whole folder — flagging anywhere it wasn't confident so you can decide. It never assigns grades or scores; it drafts the words, you keep the judgment. Use when facing a stack of essays, projects, discussion posts, lab reports, or problem sets that each need written formative feedback. Trigger phrases include "draft feedback on these", "help me give feedback", "I have a stack of essays to comment on", "grade these" (it drafts comments, never grades), "feedback in my voice", "respond to these submissions", "comment on this student's draft".

plugins.name: letter-of-rec-drafter
plugins.description: Drafts a recommendation letter from your actual notes and memories of the person, in your letter voice, shaped to the specific opportunity — and refuses to invent accomplishments you didn't give it evidence for. On first run it learns your letter voice from a past letter or two you're proud of. Then you hand it the raw material — what you genuinely remember, their CV or résumé, the job or program they're applying to — and it drafts a voice-true letter, flags any claim it couldn't ground in your evidence, and produces the length you need: full letter, short form, or a portal text-box paragraph. Missing evidence comes back as a question, never as filler. Use during recommendation-letter season or any time someone asks you for a reference. Trigger phrases include "write a rec letter", "letter of recommendation", "a student asked me for a reference", "draft a LOR", "recommendation for grad school", "reference letter for a colleague", "I need to write a rec for".

plugins.name: proposal-composer
plugins.description: Drafts a fee-anchored speaking, workshop, or consulting proposal from your own past comparable work. It pulls the closest engagements from your history, anchors the fee to what you've actually charged for similar work (never a number from thin air), assembles the proposal in your voice with your bio and session descriptions, and writes a private negotiation appendix — your floor, your walk-away, and what to trade instead of price. Drafts only; it never sends. Use when responding to an inquiry, preparing a pitch, or quoting a fee. Trigger phrases include "draft a proposal", "what should I quote", "respond to this speaking inquiry", "write a consulting proposal", "price this engagement".

plugins.name: rubric-builder
plugins.description: Turns rubric-writing from a blank-page chore into a short interview with a quality gate at the end — and hands back a formatted rubric, not a wall of chat text. It asks what the task is and what mastery looks like, drafts weighted criteria against bundled exemplar rubrics, runs a quality pass (observable criteria, no double-barreled rows, honest weightings), and produces both an instructor rubric and a plain student-facing version. Use when building a rubric, grading criteria, or a scoring guide, or to quality-check a rubric you already have. Trigger phrases include "build a rubric", "make a rubric for this assignment", "grading criteria", "scoring guide", "check my rubric".

plugins.name: session-wrap-up
plugins.description: End-of-session ritual that saves your progress before the context is lost. When a working session or phase is wrapping up, it reviews what happened, persists what matters to your notes and project memory, writes a short resume note so the next session starts warm, and flags any uncommitted version-control work. Use when finishing a phase or project, switching or ending a session, or stopping for the day. Trigger phrases include "wrap up", "wrap-up", "save our progress", "checkpoint this", "update the docs and memory", "I'm done for now", "before I go", "ending the session".

plugins.name: skill-surgeon
plugins.description: Examines, explains, and customizes the skills you already have — ones you built, ones you downloaded, ones you've forgotten. In single-skill mode it produces a full diagnostic (what the skill is for, how it triggers, the steps it follows, its parameters and dependencies, plus a check for anything surprising in third-party skills), then proposes customizations grounded in what your AI platform already knows about you and your work, and applies the edits you approve — always with a backup first. In sweep mode it audits every installed skill and returns a fleet report; which are high-value for your actual work, which overlap, which are stale, and which warrant surgery. Use whenever the user wants to understand, vet, audit, tune, personalize, or modify an existing skill — even if they don't say "skill" (e.g., "what does this slash command do", "make this tool fit how I work"). Trigger phrases include "what does this skill do", "analyze this skill", "customize this skill", "audit my skills", "what skills do I have", "skill checkup", "is this skill safe", "I downloaded this skill", "make this skill mine". For building a brand-new skill from scratch, use a skill-creation tool instead — Skill Surgeon operates only on skills that already exist.

plugins.name: source-auditor
plugins.description: Checks the citations and factual claims in a draft so fabricated sources don't slip through. It extracts every citation and checkable claim, verifies each source actually exists and actually supports the claim attached to it, and returns a verdict table — confirmed, unverifiable, or contradicted — so your manual follow-up is minutes, not an afternoon. Built for AI-drafted or AI-assisted writing, where invented references are the loudest failure mode. Use to fact-check citations, verify sources, or vet a draft you don't yet trust. Trigger phrases include "check these citations", "are these sources real", "verify the references", "fact-check this draft", "did AI make up these citations".

plugins.name: survey-synthesizer
plugins.description: Turns a pile of open-ended survey responses into themes with the respondents' own voices attached. It clusters what people actually said (not what the question hoped they'd say), keeps representative verbatim quotes on every theme, flags dissent and minority views instead of averaging them away, and is honest about what the sample can and can't support. In a file-capable tool it runs on a whole folder of exports at once — a semester of course evals in a single pass. Use to analyze open-ended responses, synthesize survey comments, or find themes in feedback. Trigger phrases include "analyze these survey responses", "synthesize this feedback", "themes in these comments", "summarize open-ended responses", "what are people saying in these evals".
